A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the Gemstones study and retain the same underlying model suite. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, supporting comparison despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: v1 reports original training results for 22 transformer configurations, learning-rate experiments, fitted scaling laws, and resource-efficiency analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original training and scaling results and adds downstream benchmarking, validation across text datasets, extrapolation tests, and leave-one-model-out analyses.

M1.justification: v2 removes the explicit width/depth-aware loss models and exhaustive architecture-search procedure developed in v1 Section 4.1 and Appendix D. It adds loss-to-benchmark-error and task-loss-to-accuracy predictors in Section 4.3. The transformer architecture, learning-rate scaling rule, and convex-hull fitting procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Dolma evaluation, v2 evaluates FineWeb, FineWeb-Edu, and DCLM-baseline. It also adds MMLU, WinoGrande, OpenBookQA, ARC-Easy/Challenge, CommonsenseQA, PIQA, SIQA, and HellaSwag evaluations. These substantially expand task and validation-distribution coverage.

E2.justification: Kaplan and Chinchilla remain the central scaling-law comparators. v2 drops the configuration-level comparisons against Gemma, Llama, and Qwen2 models accompanying v1's shape prescriptions in Figure 5 and Appendix D. Selected Qwen2.5 and Llama validation-loss references remain in the retained overtraining analysis.

E3.justification: v2 introduces benchmark evaluation at 10B-token intervals, length-normalized accuracy comparisons, held-out 2B-model extrapolation using a 1.8B cutoff, and validation-loss relative error measured over 250B–350B tokens. Leave-one-model-out fitting adds another evaluation design. The reported learning-rate validation budget also changes from 2B tokens to 1,000 steps totaling 4.2B tokens; this does not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of validation-distribution stability, larger-model extrapolation, and sensitivity to omitting individual model shapes (Section 4.3 and Appendices D–E). Conversely, v1's dedicated width/depth-law ablations, including alternative functional forms and relaxed integer constraints, disappear. Existing learning-rate, cooldown, and grid-size analyses are partly retained.

E5.justification: v2 adds minimum/maximum prescription ranges across leave-one-model-out refits in Figure 13 and error bars in benchmark Figures 8 and 15. The benchmark bars' construction is not explained. Neither version reports training-seed replication or confidence intervals, so additional repeated training runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: v2 adds benchmark scores, stable model rankings across validation corpora, and contrasting error-versus-accuracy extrapolation findings. Appendix D reports validation-loss relative errors of 0.68% when fitting all checkpoints and 0.63% when withholding the largest models; these use different fitting conditions. v1's detailed optimal-width/depth prescription results are removed, while its overspending and overtraining results remain.

T1.justification: The mathematical modeling scope changes: v1's four-term width/depth/parameter/token loss definition and alternative three-term law are absent from v2, which instead defines exponential benchmark-error and sigmoidal accuracy mappings in Equations (2)–(3). Appendix B.1 restates previously used Chinchilla mathematics rather than supplying a new derivation. Neither version contains theoretical proofs.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds optimal architectural prescriptions and the efficiency of overtraining. v2 replaces these headline contributions with evidence that deeper models improve loss and benchmark performance per FLOP while wider models train faster under its parallelism setup. The abstract also drops the claim that Gemstones is the most comprehensive open-source scaling-law dataset.

C2.justification: v2 interprets cross-dataset rank stability as supporting alternative validation distributions, attributes benchmark-fit variability to architectural diversity, and links leave-one-out robustness to convex-hull fitting. It identifies poor accuracy extrapolation and develops the distinction between compute-efficient depth and time-efficient width. The existing limitation concerning parallelism-dependent timing results is retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies Dolma 1.7, documents task-loss construction and benchmark checkpoint selection, and explains recalibrating GPU-hour analyses using measured step times on other hardware. Most architecture, optimizer, initialization, and FLOP-counting details are retained. v1's promise of a later training-code release is dropped, without establishing an actual availability change.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around downstream scaling through Gadre and Bhagia, depth benefits and pruning through Gemma 2, Zuo, and Gromov, and newer depth-transfer work. It also positions Gemstones against a gap associated with Pile-trained model suites. Earlier literature is largely retained, sometimes relocated.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution statements, related-work narrative, and experimental organization are substantially rewritten. Architecture and learning-rate explanations move into Appendix A, while overspending and overtraining move into Appendices H–I. The appendices are extensively reorganized around the revised narrative.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, adds numerical sensitivity tables and benchmark, extrapolation, and uncertainty displays, and removes the extensive shape-prescription figure series. Several existing figures are resized or relocated, including the retained overspending and overtraining plots.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation: v1 lacked direct downstream evaluation and held-out extrapolation tests, whereas Section 4.3 and Appendices D–E test practical performance, distribution stability, extrapolation, and model-selection sensitivity. Reporting poor accuracy extrapolation also exposes an important boundary. Removing the width/depth-law specification makes the retained overtraining analysis less self-contained, and benchmark error bars remain unexplained, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger support for the paper's central empirical contributions.
